In [[mathematics]], the class of '''Muckenhoupt weights''' {{math|''A<sub>p</sub>''}} consists of those weights {{mvar|ω}} for which the [[Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator]] is bounded on {{math|''L<sup>p</sup>''(''dω'')}}. Specifically, we consider functions {{math|&thinsp;''f''&thinsp;}} on {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} and their associated [[maximal function]]s {{math|''M''(&thinsp;''f''&thinsp;)}} defined as

:<math> M(f)(x) = \sup_{r>0} \frac{1}{r^n} \int_{B_r(x)} |f|,</math>

where {{math|''B<sub>r</sub>''(''x'')}} is the ball in {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} with radius {{mvar|r}} and center at {{mvar|x}}. Let {{math|1 ≤ ''p'' < ∞}}, we wish to characterise the functions {{math|''ω'' : '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> → [0, ∞)}} for which we have a bound

:<math> \int |M(f)(x)|^p \, \omega(x) dx \leq C \int |f|^p \, \omega(x)\, dx,</math>

where {{mvar|C}} depends only on {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|ω}}. This was first done by [[Benjamin Muckenhoupt]].<ref>{{cite journal|last = Muckenhoupt | first = Benjamin| title = Weighted norm inequalities for the Hardy maximal function | journal = Transactions of the American Mathematical Society | pages = 207–226| year = 1972 | volume = 165| doi = 10.1090/S0002-9947-1972-0293384-6| doi-access = free}}</ref>

==Definition==
For a fixed {{math|1 < ''p'' < ∞}}, we say that a weight {{math|''ω'' : '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> → [0, ∞)}} belongs to {{math|''A<sub>p</sub>''}} if {{mvar|ω}} is locally integrable and there is a constant {{mvar|C}} such that, for all balls {{mvar|B}} in {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}, we have

:<math>\left(\frac{1}{|B|} \int_B \omega(x) \, dx \right)\left(\frac{1}{|B|} \int_B \omega(x)^{-\frac{q}{p}} \, dx \right)^\frac{p}{q} \leq C < \infty,</math>

where {{math|{{!}}''B''{{!}}}} is the [[Lebesgue measure]] of {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|q}} is a [[real number]] such that: {{math|{{sfrac|1|''p''}} + {{sfrac|1|''q''}} {{=}} 1}}.

We say {{math|''ω'' : '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> → [0, ∞)}} belongs to {{math|''A''<sub>1</sub>}} if there exists some {{mvar|C}} such that

: <math>\frac{1}{|B|} \int_B \omega(y) \, dy \leq C\omega(x), </math>

for almost every {{math|''x'' ∈ ''B''}} and all balls {{mvar|B}}.<ref name = bible>{{cite book|last = Stein | first = Elias |author-link=Elias M. Stein | title = Harmonic Analysis | chapter = 5 | publisher = Princeton University Press| year = 1993 }}</ref>

==Equivalent characterizations==
This following result is a fundamental result in the study of Muckenhoupt weights.

:'''Theorem.''' Let {{math|1 < ''p'' < ∞}}. A weight {{mvar|ω}} is in {{math|''A<sub>p</sub>''}} [[if and only if]] any one of the following hold.<ref name = bible/>

::(a) The [[Hardy–Littlewood maximal function]] is bounded on {{math|''L<sup>p</sup>''(''ω''(''x'')''dx'')}}, that is

:::<math> \int |M(f)(x)|^p \, \omega(x)\, dx \leq C \int |f|^p \, \omega(x)\, dx,</math>

::for some {{mvar|C}} which only depends on {{mvar|p}} and the constant {{mvar|A}} in the above definition.

::(b) There is a constant {{mvar|c}} such that for any locally integrable function {{math|&thinsp;''f''&thinsp;}} on {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}, and all balls {{mvar|B}}:

:::<math>(f_B)^p \leq \frac{c}{\omega(B)} \int_B f(x)^p \, \omega(x)\,dx,</math>

::where:

:::<math>f_B = \frac{1}{|B|}\int_B f, \qquad \omega(B) = \int_B \omega(x)\,dx.</math>

Equivalently:

:'''Theorem.''' Let {{math|1 < ''p'' < ∞}}, then {{math|''w'' {{=}} ''e<sup>φ</sup>'' ∈ ''A<sub>p</sub>''}} if and only if both of the following hold:

::<math> \sup_{B}\frac{1}{|B|}\int_{B}e^{\varphi-\varphi_B}dx<\infty </math>
::<math> \sup_{B}\frac{1}{|B|}\int_{B}e^{-\frac{\varphi-\varphi_B}{p-1}}dx<\infty. </math>

This equivalence can be verified by using [[Jensen's Inequality]].

==Reverse Hölder inequalities and {{math|''A''<sub>∞</sub>}}==
The main tool in the proof of the above equivalence is the following result.<ref name=bible/> The following statements are equivalent

#{{math|''ω'' ∈ ''A<sub>p</sub>''}} for some {{math|1 ≤ ''p'' < ∞}}.
#There exist {{math|0 < ''δ'', ''γ'' < 1}} such that for all balls {{mvar|B}} and subsets {{math|''E'' ⊂ ''B''}}, {{math|{{!}}''E''{{!}} ≤ ''γ''&thinsp;{{!}}''B''{{!}}}} implies {{math|''ω''(''E'') ≤ ''δ''&thinsp;''ω''(''B'')}}.
#There exist {{math|1 < ''q''}} and {{mvar|c}} (both depending on {{mvar|ω}}) such that for all balls {{mvar|B}} we have:
:: <math>\frac{1}{|B|} \int_{B} \omega^q \leq \left(\frac{c}{|B|} \int_{B} \omega \right)^q.</math>

We call the inequality in the third formulation a reverse Hölder inequality as the reverse inequality follows for any non-negative function directly from [[Hölder's inequality]]. If any of the three equivalent conditions above hold we say {{mvar|ω}} belongs to {{math|''A''<sub>∞</sub>}}.

==Weights and BMO==
The definition of an {{math|''A<sub>p</sub>''}} weight and the reverse Hölder inequality indicate that such a weight cannot degenerate or grow too quickly. This property can be phrased equivalently in terms of how much the logarithm of the weight oscillates:

:(a) If {{math|''w'' ∈ ''A<sub>p</sub>'', (''p'' ≥ 1),}} then {{math|log(''w'') ∈ BMO}} (i.e. {{math|log(''w'')}} has [[bounded mean oscillation]]).

:(b) If {{math|&thinsp;''f''&thinsp; ∈ BMO}}, then for sufficiently small {{math|''δ'' > 0}}, we have {{math|''e<sup>δf</sup>'' ∈ ''A<sub>p</sub>''}} for some {{math|''p'' ≥ 1}}.

This equivalence can be established by using the exponential characterization of weights above, Jensen's inequality, and the [[John–Nirenberg inequality]].

Note that the smallness assumption on {{math|''δ'' > 0}} in part (b) is necessary for the result to be true, as {{math|−log{{!}}''x''{{!}} ∈ BMO}}, but:

:<math>e^{-\log|x|}=\frac{1}{e^{\log|x|}} = \frac{1}{|x|}</math>

is not in any {{math|''A<sub>p</sub>''}}.

==Further properties==
Here we list a few miscellaneous properties about weights, some of which can be verified from using the definitions, others are nontrivial results:

:<math>A_1 \subseteq A_p \subseteq A_\infty, \qquad 1\leq p\leq\infty.</math>

:<math>A_\infty = \bigcup_{p<\infty}A_p.</math>

:If {{math|''w'' ∈ ''A<sub>p</sub>''}}, then {{math|''w''&thinsp;''dx''}} defines a [[doubling measure]]: for any ball {{mvar|B}}, if {{math|2''B''}} is the ball of twice the radius, then {{math|''w''(2''B'') ≤ ''Cw''(''B'')}} where {{math|''C'' > 1}} is a constant depending on {{mvar|w}}.

:If {{math|''w'' ∈ ''A<sub>p</sub>''}}, then there is {{math|''δ'' > 1}} such that {{math|''w<sup>δ</sup>'' ∈ ''A<sub>p</sub>''}}.

:If {{math|''w'' ∈ ''A''<sub>∞</sub>}}, then there is {{math|''δ'' > 0}} and weights <math>w_1,w_2\in A_1</math> such that <math>w=w_1 w_2^{-\delta}</math>.<ref>{{cite journal| last = Jones | first = Peter W.|title = Factorization of {{math|''A<sub>p</sub>''}} weights| journal = Ann. of Math. |series =  2 | volume = 111 | pages = 511–530 | year = 1980| doi = 10.2307/1971107  | issue = 3| jstor = 1971107}}</ref>

==Boundedness of singular integrals==
It is not only the Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator that is bounded on these weighted {{math|''L<sup>p</sup>''}} spaces. In fact, any [[singular integrals|Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operator]] is also bounded on these spaces.<ref name = grafakos>{{cite book | last = Grafakos | first = Loukas | title = Classical and Modern Fourier Analysis | chapter = 9 | publisher = Pearson Education, Inc. | place = New Jersey| year = 2004 }}</ref> Let us describe a simpler version of this here.<ref name = bible/> Suppose we have an operator {{mvar|T}} which is bounded on {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>(''dx'')}}, so we have

: <math>\forall f \in C^{\infty}_c : \qquad \|T(f)\|_{L^2} \leq C\|f\|_{L^2}.</math>

Suppose also that we can realise {{mvar|T}} as convolution against a kernel {{mvar|K}} in the following sense: if {{math|&thinsp;''f''&thinsp;, ''g''}} are smooth with disjoint support, then:

: <math>\int g(x) T(f)(x) \, dx = \iint g(x) K(x-y) f(y) \, dy\,dx.</math>

Finally we assume a size and smoothness condition on the kernel {{mvar|K}}:

: <math> \forall x \neq 0, \forall |\alpha| \leq 1 : \qquad \left |\partial^{\alpha} K \right | \leq C |x|^{-n-\alpha}.</math>

Then, for each {{math|1 < ''p'' < ∞}} and {{math|''ω'' ∈ ''A<sub>p</sub>''}}, {{mvar|T}} is a [[bounded operator]] on {{math|''L<sup>p</sup>''(''ω''(''x'')''dx'')}}. That is, we have the estimate

: <math>\int |T(f)(x)|^p \, \omega(x)\,dx \leq C \int |f(x)|^p \, \omega(x)\, dx,</math>

for all {{math|&thinsp;''f''&thinsp;}} for which the right-hand side is finite.

===A converse result===
If, in addition to the three conditions above, we assume the non-degeneracy condition on the kernel {{mvar|K}}: For a fixed [[unit vector]] {{math|''u''<sub>0</sub>}}

: <math>|K(x)| \geq a |x|^{-n}</math>

whenever <math>x = t \dot u_0</math> with {{math|−∞ < ''t'' < ∞}}, then we have a converse. If we know

: <math>\int |T(f)(x)|^p \, \omega(x)\,dx \leq C \int |f(x)|^p \, \omega(x)\, dx,</math>

for some fixed {{math|1 < ''p'' < ∞}} and some {{mvar|ω}}, then {{math|''ω'' ∈ ''A<sub>p</sub>''}}.<ref name = bible/>

==Weights and quasiconformal mappings==
For {{math|''K'' > 1}}, a {{mvar|K}}-[[quasiconformal mapping]] is a [[homeomorphism]] {{math|&thinsp;''f''&thinsp; : '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> →'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} such that

:<math>f\in W^{1,2}_{loc}(\mathbf{R}^n), \quad \text{ and } \quad \frac{\|Df(x)\|^n}{J(f,x)}\leq K, </math>

where {{math|''Df''&thinsp;(''x'')}} is the [[derivative]] of {{math|&thinsp;''f''&thinsp;}} at {{mvar|x}} and {{math|''J''(&thinsp;''f''&thinsp;, ''x'') {{=}} det(''Df''&thinsp;(''x''))}} is the [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian]].

A theorem of Gehring<ref>{{cite journal|last = Gehring | first = F. W.| title = The L<sup>p</sup>-integrability of the partial derivatives of a quasiconformal mapping| journal = Acta Math. | volume = 130 | pages = 265–277 | year = 1973| doi = 10.1007/BF02392268| doi-access = free}}</ref> states that for all {{mvar|K}}-quasiconformal functions {{math|&thinsp;''f''&thinsp; : '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> →'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}, we have {{math|''J''(&thinsp;''f''&thinsp;, ''x'') ∈ ''A<sub>p</sub>''}}, where {{mvar|p}} depends on {{mvar|K}}.

==Harmonic measure==
If you have a simply connected domain {{math|Ω ⊆ '''C'''}}, we say its boundary curve {{math|Γ {{=}} ∂Ω}} is {{mvar|K}}-chord-arc if for any two points {{math|''z'', ''w''}} in {{math|Γ}} there is a curve {{math|''γ'' ⊆ Γ}} connecting {{mvar|z}} and {{mvar|w}} whose length is no more than {{math|''K''{{!}}''z'' − ''w''{{!}}}}. For a domain with such a boundary and for any {{math|''z''<sub>0</sub>}} in {{math|Ω}}, the [[harmonic measure]] {{math|''w''( ⋅ ) {{=}} ''w''(''z''<sub>0</sub>, Ω, ⋅)}} is absolutely continuous with respect to one-dimensional [[Hausdorff measure]] and its [[Radon–Nikodym derivative]] is in {{math|''A''<sub>∞</sub>}}.<ref>{{cite book| last=Garnett | first=John|author2=Marshall, Donald | title = Harmonic Measure| publisher = Cambridge University Press | year = 2008}}</ref> (Note that in this case, one needs to adapt the definition of weights to the case where the underlying measure is one-dimensional Hausdorff measure).
